The Return of China…or maybe not yet

1⃣Pre-crisis, looking at the export data trends, it looked like mogas export volumes were more stable and range-bound than jet and diesel exports. This suggests that mogas is the main fuel that China needs to keep as security for domestic plans, and middle distillates are the resultant barrels.

2⃣China has shown they are very geopolitically and economically sensitive, emerging as the dominant buyer during the fifth ADNOC tender for July and August loaders when the ceasefire was in place, and getting very good discounts for those crudes.

3⃣They also benefited from additional crude escaping the Strait of Hormuz in June that would have arrived in 2H July into China, allowing more refined products in the supply chain than earlier committed. This translates to higher refined products in July & Aug.

4⃣However, when the US-Iran tensions flared up again in early July, China was not awarded any cargoes in the sixth ADNOC tender and in fact were reselling some of the Upper Zakum crude they bought for a good profit. They picked up some cargoes in the seventh ADNOC tender for Aug/Sep/Oct loaders.

5⃣Saudi allocations for August loaders were around 10 mb which is likely the lowest since the start of the crisis. We will need to see the Saudi term allocations for September loaders to see if they are going to sustain a higher crude purchasing signal in order to export more products. 

6⃣We have not seen a pick-up in WAF crude buying activity from China, but hearing more Russian crude is headed there via the Arctic route and more ESPO purchases from Sinopec.

Thus my view is that the actual refined product exports for July and August is more a result of that incremental runs from the Strait of Hormuz. The risk of getting lower runs due to crude arrival uncertainties may result in a lower actual export quantity than the approved quotas for August.

El Niño and its impact on the global energy system

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a record high for the time of year, causing forecasters to predict a very strong El Niño will form in the final months of 2026.  

Surface temperatures averaged about 29.6°C last week, up from 26.6°C at the same time last year, according to data from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Temperatures were 1°C higher than the previous record for the time of year and 2.7°C above the long-term seasonal average, indicating exceptional warmth across the region. 

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific are a key driver of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, the single largest influence on weather patterns at seasonal scale worldwide. 

ENSO has significant impacts on the energy production and consumption – including hurricane formation in the Atlantic, winter temperatures and heating demand in the United States, and hydroelectric generation in South America ...

text: Now would be a good time for the BOJ to step in again. With the dollar already under pressure and U.S. yields falling, it is much easier to push the ball downhill than uphill

Gold jumps to a 2½-month high near USD 4,460, supported by falling bond yields and a 0.6% drop in the dollar, which has also slipped to a 2½-month low. The combination of lower yields and a weaker dollar providing fresh tailwind, reinforcing the recovery seen since early August.

The big technical test remains the 200-day moving average, currently around USD 4,510. A sustained break above this key trend indicator would strengthen the technical outlook while signalling that the correction from the January peak may finally have run its course.

The BIG question now is how the market interprets these moves. The increase in Treasury buybacks is tiny relative to a roughly USD 40 trillion federal debt pile, but the signal may matter more than the size.

Taken together, the larger long-end buybacks and the potential expansion of the Fed’s FIMA repo facility look increasingly like measures designed to limit forced selling of Treasuries and contain upward pressure on long-term yields. FIMA allows foreign central banks to raise dollars against their Treasury holdings rather than selling those securities outright, thereby providing dollar liquidity while temporarily expanding the Fed’s balance sheet.

In that sense, there is an element of Operation Twist by another route: support the long end, improve liquidity and reduce the risk that foreign reserve managers become forced sellers at precisely the wrong time.

That combination is potentially bearish for the dollar, particularly if markets interpret it as another step towards greater official support for the Treasury market and, ultimately, easier financial conditions. That, at least, appears to be the initial market interpretation: yields down, equities and gold up, and the dollar weaker.

The maximum size of operations covering the 10–20-year and 20–30-year sectors will rise from USD 2 billion to at least USD 4 billion per operation.

Small potatoes in the context of the overall Treasury market, but the signal matters, particularly at a time when long-end yields have surged amid growing concerns about fiscal sustainability, heavy issuance and weakening foreign demand.

The announcement suggests the Treasury is becoming increasingly sensitive to liquidity conditions and upward pressure on long-term borrowing costs. That helps explain the immediate market reaction: lower yields providing relief to equities while supporting gold through lower real-rate pressure.

Industrial metals: #Copper retreated from near-record highs after one of the largest squeezes seen in the market eased somewhat on Tuesday, as traders including Trafigura Group made significant deliveries of metal to the London Metal Exchange. The deliveries provided some relief after a recent surge in shipments to the US had sharply reduced LME inventories that underpin global benchmark contracts, contributing to extreme tightness in nearby supply. In New York, High Grade copper trades near USD 6.55 per pound, down from above USD 6.80 on Monday.
Agriculture: Raw #sugar futures in New York rose to a 14-month high on Tuesday and are now up around 20% this month, supported by global supply concerns as El Niño threatens to reduce harvests across key Asian producers. Arabica #coffee meanwhile rose to a six-month high, supported by delays to the Brazilian harvest and disruption following a deadly earthquake in Colombia, slowing the flow of beans to the market and adding to concerns about near-term availability.Crude
